children: Conway propane could remain at a wider discount to the Mont Belvieu product through the end of winter demand season compared with recent trends, spot prices and forward price projections currently indicate.
Usually, a narrowing of the north-south spread, or Mont Belvieu's premium over Conway, is expected every fall, and futures markets show the process has begun for this year.

This narrowing is driven by differing seasonal dynamics in Gulf Coast and Midcontinent markets, respectively proxied by the export-benchmark Mont Belvieu natural gas liquids hub on the outskirts of Houston and the smaller Conway hub in landlocked Kansas.
But this year, the gap is wider.

The month-to-date average price as of Sept. 18 for spot propane traded out of Enterprise Products Partners caverns in Mont Belvieu (labeled non-TET propane) stood 7.31cts/gal higher than the Conway product, at 80.83cts/gal versus 73.52cts/gal. For the whole month of September in 2025, this premium was 0.66ct/gal.

The month-to-date average spot price of Mont Belvieu TET propane, or barrels traded out of Energy Transfer caverns, was 3.1cts/gal higher than non-TET on Sept. 18, meaning the TET-Conway spread was even wider.
A propane trade participant in the Midwest cited two reasons why physical and paper markets both indicate wider spreads this year.
"El Niño causing a warm winter," he told OPIS. "And more importantly, the market doesn't see the Iran-U.S. and Ukraine-Russia issues going away.
"So they believe [propane] exports will still be at a premium compared with domestic U.S. sales throughout winter," he said.
The second belief is also manifest in a slightly backwardated Mont Belvieu propane curve, which is based on the TET product that is used in paper markets.
Values published in the Sept. 18 OPIS NGL Forwards Report projected TET futures dipping from 84.125cts/gal in October to 81.0625cts/gal in February.

This projected weakening partly aligns with a backwardated curve for U.S. crude, the commodity with which propane is organically linked and with whose price it remains structurally correlated. But crude is projected to drop more sharply, lifting Mont Belvieu propane futures' projected price percentage to the relevant crude contracts from around 36% in October to 40% in February.
Forward prices also are the market's signal to traders that "it is not worth their while to store propane," said Peter Fasullo, principal of Houston consultancy En*Vantage Inc.

"Forward price curves in both crude and propane reflect the underlying strength of export demand," Fasullo said. "In financial terms, this means selling the barrels immediately in export markets is better than storing them through winter, paying for the storage, and then ending up with an even lower price at the other end."

Meanwhile, Conway propane futures in the Sept. 18 Forwards Report were projected to rise from 75.75cts/gal in October to 79cts/gal in February. In this manner, the north-south spread was projected to narrow from 8.375cts/gal to 2.0625cts/gal.
Based on monthly average physical prices for Mont Belvieu non-TET and Conway propane from OPIS data, the north-south spread had dropped from 4.22cts/gal in Oct. 2025 to 1.56cts/gal in Feb. 2026.

The U.S. was facing a relative propane shortage in 2022, and Conway propane traded at a premium to Mont Belvieu in the final four months, ranging from 0.81cts/gal in September to 3.33cts/gal in December.
One needs to understand regional dynamics to make sense of this north-south relationship.

Midwest propane demand is concentrated in colder months, and a higher proportion of homes in the Midwest and Plains regions uses propane for winter heating. Propane also has a provisional four- to six-week demand window in the agricultural heartland from mid-October through Thanksgiving, as farmers might use it to dry crops if there is less sunshine or more rain during harvest season.
During the rest of the year, surplus Midwest barrels are free to flow south if needed, and thence to global markets via export-thirsty Gulf Coast waterfronts.
An "open" north-south arbitrage keeps such flows fiscally feasible, as it leaves Midwest sellers with sufficient margins after deducting pipeline transport costs.
Gulf Coast propane is tethered to exports. This demand is inelastic; laden ships embark year-round like clockwork. That means the Mont Belvieu price displays minimal seasonal variations.
Fasullo projects "below-average" crop-drying demand this fall. And there really is "no concern about supply," he said.

Energy Information Administration data for the week ended Sept. 11 showed PADD2 (the Midcontinent region) propane-propylene stockpiles stood at 26.259 million bbl, comparable with the 26.055 million bbl reported for the corresponding week last year and 3.8% higher than the 2021-2025 average of 25.307 million bbl.
In contrast, PADD3 (the Gulf Coast region) is drowning in propane. This region houses most of the country's NGL storage capacity and sends out roughly three-fourths of waterborne propane exports.
EIA-reported PADD3 stocks stood at 69.626 million bbl on Sept. 11, 17.9% higher than last year's 59.062 million bbl and 38.4% higher than the 2021-2025 average of 50.306 million bbl.
This means most of America's current propane glut — nationwide Sept. 11 stocks of 109.092 million bbl were a historical high — is clogged up along the Gulf Coast.
This overhang is a culmination of three forces that built up steadily over the past decade.

EIA weekly data show propane-propylene production burgeoned from around 1.7 million b/d in early 2017 to nearly 3 million b/d at present. Meanwhile, stateside propane consumption on an annually normalized basis remained unmoved around 1 million b/d.
This obliged exports to pick up the slack, which they did. These flows averaged less than 1 million b/d until 2017 or so, and currently average 2 million-2.1 million b/d.
But there is a catch: Exports now don't have much room to the upside until scheduled waterfront expansions enter service during 2027 and beyond.

U.S. liquefied petroleum gas waterfronts through this spring were already operating near full capacity, making it difficult for propane exports to rise beyond a certain level. But export docks have striven in recent years to add marginal volumes by improving loading efficiencies and tweaking other variables. EIA weekly data show propane exports averaged 1.757 million b/d in 2024 and 1.862 million b/d in 2025.

Some relief on the capacity front finally came in April this year, when Enterprise debuted its Neches River propane export facility on the Sabine-Neches Waterway outside Beaumont, Texas, some 100 miles east of Houston.

EIA weekly data from the beginning of January through April 10 this year show propane exports averaged 1.902 million b/d. In the weeks from April 17 to Sept. 11, outflows averaged 2.065 million b/d, lifting the year-to-date average through Sept. 11 to 1.999 million b/d.
Meanwhile, geopolitics are screaming "the more propane America can export, the better."
Through Feb. 2026, the U.S. was already the world's biggest LPG (propane and butane) exporter, sending out 2.6 million-2.7 million b/d in combined volumes.

Middle East producers as a bloc exported 1.5 million b/d of LPG in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency. Major importers, including notable newcomers like India, turned to the U.S. for replacement supplies after these flows were completely choked off in the early stages of the Persian Gulf conflict.

Middle East exporters have salvaged some lost volumes since then. But these flows remain scattershot and sporadic, with Strait of Hormuz realities always casting a dark shadow. And the U.S. is unable to fully capitalize.
"There is just not enough [additional] capacity to move what is needed off U.S. waters," the Midwest source said.
A second Midwest trade watcher cited this constraint as a reason why the Mont Belvieu price is stagnating even as the north-south arbitrage remains theoretically open.
"I think it has to do with warm weather expected in the fourth quarter and high demand on exports throughout winter," this contact said.
"We need some [cold] weather demand to pull barrels out of Belvieu [for U.S. consumption] and tighten [the supply picture] up."

Overland Park, Kan.-based Westlark Advisors summarized this jumbled situation in a commentary published on Sept. 14. "A growing issue for the North American propane sector is higher inventory levels for longer," the firm wrote.

"With the prospect of a record El Niño for this winter, record high inventory levels and steady production growth, the U.S. could end the 2026-2027 winter with one of the highest (if not the highest) inventory levels. Normally this would be bearish on prices — but we simply see this as limiting the upside caused by a massive global LPG shortfall."
